title: Evaluate Sums With Parentheses
statement:
You get a valid arithmetic expression expr as text. It contains non-negative whole numbers, +, -, parentheses and spaces. Return its value.

  • - can also be a unary minus: at the very start, or right after an opening parenthesis, as in -(2 + 3) or (-4).
  • + is only ever binary.
  • Operators of the same level are applied left to right.

Do not use a built-in evaluator such as eval. Every intermediate value fits in a signed 32-bit integer.

examples.why: The parentheses are worked out first: 3 − 1 = 2, then 7 − 2 = 5.
The leading minus negates the whole group: −10 + 12 = 2.
Left to right: (10 − 2) − 3. Grouping from the right, 10 − (2 − 3), would give 11.

constraints: Every number and every intermediate result fits in 32 bits
hints: Without parentheses this is easy: keep a running total and the sign of the next number.
A parenthesis starts a fresh sub-total. When it closes, that sub-total gets added to the outer total with the sign that stood in front of the '('. What do you need to remember across the parenthesis?
On '(', push the current total and the pending sign onto a stack and restart from 0. On ')', finish the inner total, pop, and combine: outer + sign · inner.

explain.intuition:
With only + and -, an expression is just a sum of signed numbers. Walk left to right, keep total and the sign (+1 or −1) of the next number, and add sign · number whenever a number ends.

Parentheses interrupt that walk. Opening one means "put the current work aside and start a new sum". A stack is exactly a pile of work put aside: push total and the sign in front of the bracket, start again at 0, and when the bracket closes, pop and fold the inner result back in. Unary minus needs no special case: at the start or after ( the total is 0, so -x reads as 0 − x.
steps: + or -: add sign · num to total, reset num, set sign to +1 or −1.
): add sign · num to total, reset num, pop the saved sign and total, and set total = savedTotal + savedSign · total.
At the end add the last sign · num and return total.
pitfalls: Reading numbers one digit at a time and forgetting multi-digit numbers like 100.
Forgetting to flush num into total before a ) or at the end of the string.
Treating subtraction as right-associative, or applying the sign in front of a bracket to only the first number inside it.

solutions.title: Stack of saved totals
solutions.idea: Keep a running total and a pending sign. Each '(' saves both on a stack and starts over; each ')' folds the inner total back into the saved one.

solutions.title: Stack of effective signs
solutions.idea: Every number ends up added or subtracted from one grand total. Its final sign is its own sign times the signs of all brackets around it, so keep a stack of those combined signs.

followups: Add * and /, which bind tighter than + and -. How does the stack change?
Write it as a recursive-descent parser with one function per grammar rule. What limits the nesting depth then?
